sentences.text: Dunkleosteus possessed dermal bone armor plates covering its skull and the front half of its trunk.
This armored head featured jaws equipped with unusual blade-like teeth.
D. terrelli is the type species and is considered the largest and best-known species of Dunkleosteus.
A 4.6-meter-long adult Dunkleosteus terrelli was estimated to weigh 665 kilograms based on a shark-like body plan.
Using an ellipsoid volumetric method, a typical 3.41-meter-long adult Dunkleosteus was estimated to weigh 950 to 1200 kilograms, while the largest 4.1-meter individual weighed 1494 to 1764 kilograms.
A specimen of Dunkleosteus and a Titanichthys show damage attributed to puncture wounds from the bony fangs of other Dunkleosteus.
Dunkleosteus fossils were first discovered in 1867 by Jay Terrell, an amateur paleontologist who found them in cliffs along Lake Erie near Sheffield Lake, Ohio.
The genus Dunkleosteus was described by Lehman in 1956.
Biomechanical modeling suggests Dunkleosteus could open its jaws in 20 milliseconds and complete the process in 50 to 60 milliseconds.

Researchers suggested that the pressures generated by Dunkleosteus's bite were sufficient to puncture or cut dermal armor, indicating it preyed on armored free-swimming organisms like ammonites and other placoderms.
Calculations indicate the front blades of Dunkleosteus bit with a pressure of 5363 newtons, while the lateral blades exerted 4414 newtons.
Studies show that juvenile Dunkleosteus had lower jaws proportionally as robust as adults, indicating they could produce high bite forces and shear resistant prey tissue from a young age.
Evidence from other placoderms suggests some may have been viviparous, including findings of what appears to be an umbilical cord.

A 2017 study reconstructed the caudal fin of Dunkleosteus terrelli with a strong ventral lobe, high aspect ratio, and narrow peduncle, differing from previous anguilliform reconstructions based on other placoderms.
Like all arthrodires, Dunkleosteus had an epaxial articulation between the dorsal plates and the skull, allowing it to raise its head upward to easily hunt large prey.
Some skull and thoracic shield fossils show cannibalistic tendencies, evidenced by bite marks matching its own dentition that did not heal.
No fossil material has been found for the rest of the body, indicating its vertebrae were cartilaginous or poorly ossified, explaining its fragility for fossilization, analogous to sharks.
Jean-Pierre Lehman named the genus Dunkleosteus in 1956 to honor David Dunkle, a former curator at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.
Dunkleosteus is classified as a member of the class Placodermi, order Arthrodira, suborder Brachythoraci, family Dunkleosteidae, and superfamily Dunkleosteoidea.
Dunkleosteus belongs to the family Dinichthyidae, which was named based on the genus Dinichthys.
The genus Dunkleosteus is currently defined as a wastebasket taxon containing large, evolutionarily derived dunkleosteoid arthrodires.
Dunkleosteus was an extinct genus of large arthrodire fish that lived during the Late Devonian period, approximately 382 to 358 million years ago.
Dunkleosteus lived during the Late Devonian period, approximately 380 to 360 million years ago, in the Frasnian and Famennian stages.
Dunkleosteus lived for approximately 20 million years, from the Late Givetian to Late Famennian of the Upper Devonian.
Dunkleosteus was a pelagic fish that inhabited open waters and served as one of the first vertebrate apex predators in any ecosystem.
This predator likely occupied the top of its ecosystem's food chain, earning the title of superpredator.
The scientific validity of several of the ten described Dunkleosteus species remains unclear.
Many researchers and authorities consider D. marsaisi to be a synonym of D. terrelli.
It is debated whether lengths of 5 meters or more for Dunkleosteus terrelli are accurate, as most such estimates lack quantitative or statistical backing.
In 2025, Engelman and colleagues challenged the suction feeding hypothesis, arguing that the underlying models did not accurately reflect Dunkleosteus anatomy.
Engelman et al. (2025) suggested that Dunkleosteus had more cartilage in its skull than previously thought, allowing a jaw gape angle of at least 65 to 70 degrees.
